title: Personal Project Academic Integrity: A Student Guide
summary: Personal Project academic integrity for MYP Year 5: learn to cite sources, use AI transparently, receive feedback, and show that your work is truly yours.
body_markdown:
**Personal Project academic integrity** means acknowledging help and borrowed material while keeping the project’s thinking, decisions and final work your own. You may research, consult experts, receive feedback and use approved tools, provided you follow your school’s rules and credit those contributions.


Imagine a hypothetical MYP Year 5 student named Maya designing a website to help teenagers reduce food waste. Her choices, revisions and unsuccessful experiments should reveal her learning. Integrity begins with her first search, not a final citation check.


If you are defining your project, start with this[guide to the MYP Personal Project](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-personal-project) .


### Your academic integrity checklist


Before submitting, check:


- Is the thinking and final work mine?
- Have I acknowledged borrowed words, facts, images, code and ideas?
- Have I followed my school’s citation style and AI policy?
- Is significant feedback documented without someone else rewriting my work?
- Does my process evidence show how the project developed?
- Have I checked both the product and report for missing references?


### What Personal Project academic integrity means


The[IB academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) expects authentic work and ethical use of information and artificial intelligence tools. It distinguishes legitimate collaboration from collusion, where submitted work is not sufficiently individual or unique.


Maya does not need to discover every fact about food waste herself. She needs to evaluate existing knowledge and make her own design decisions.


Situation Academically responsible action


Maya copies a definition exactly Use quotation marks and an in-text citation


Maya explains a source in her own words Cite the borrowed idea


She uses an online photograph Check permission or licensing and provide attribution


A friend suggests changing the navigation Record the feedback and explain her own decision


She includes AI-generated wording Follow school rules and acknowledge the output


A parent rewrites a report paragraph Do not submit it as Maya’s writing


The useful distinction is **assistance versus authorship** . Assistance supports your thinking; authorship supplies it.


A student claims to have grown a plant while the sun politely asks for acknowledgement


### Research without losing ownership


Maya creates a source log recording each source’s creator, title, publication, date, link, access date and useful ideas. She marks whether she quoted, paraphrased or merely consulted it.


This prevents a familiar problem: remembering a statistic but forgetting its origin. RevisionDojo’s guide to the[MYP academic honesty policy](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-myp-academic-honesty-policy-what-students-should-know) offers further guidance on citation and source tracking.


Changing a few words does not make an idea original. Understand the material, close the source, explain the point independently and cite its origin. Compare your version with the original to catch wording copied unintentionally.


Keep source notes separate from your own observations. For example, Maya might label an entry “website advice” and another “my testing result.” This helps her distinguish a borrowed recommendation from evidence she collected herself when writing the report.


Acknowledgement also extends beyond writing. Code, templates, recipes, musical samples and survey questions may need credit. Review these[common Personal Project mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-myp-personal-project-mistakes-e0513f75) when checking less obvious sources.


### Using AI transparently


AI use depends on your school’s rules, the task and how you use the output. Ask your supervisor before relying on it.


The IB’s[statement on AI in assessment](https://www.ibo.org/news/news-about-the-ib/statement-from-the-ib-about-chatgpt-and-artificial-intelligence-in-assessment-and-education/) says AI-generated material cannot be presented as your own work. Included material must be credited in the text and appropriately referenced in the bibliography.


Suppose Maya asks AI to suggest website categories. If permitted, she should retain relevant prompts and output, explain how she evaluated suggestions and acknowledge the tool as required. She remains responsible for checking claims and references.


Having AI write her reflection creates a deeper problem: reflection should demonstrate her learning. Acknowledgement alone does not make every use acceptable.


Before accepting a suggestion, ask whether you understand it well enough to explain your choice. If Maya cannot explain generated code, she should investigate how it works before including it. A working feature alone does not demonstrate her understanding.


RevisionDojo’s **AI Chat** and grading tools can help identify unclear reasoning. Use feedback within school rules, then make revisions independently.


### Feedback, supervision and collaboration


Maya’s supervisor asks why her homepage contains so much text and whether her success criteria can be tested. These questions help without supplying answers.


Constructive feedback identifies weaknesses, asks questions and points toward useful resources. The student retains responsibility for the wording, analysis and decisions.


A tutor may explain citation principles but should not manufacture Maya’s analysis. A friend may test the website but should not secretly build its central features. Discuss practical assistance with your supervisor, especially when a project requires specialist equipment or skills.


Record significant feedback and your response. Read the[Personal Project supervision guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/supervising-a-personal-project-teacher-tips-and-best-practices) to understand constructive support.


### Build evidence as you work


Dated drafts, sketches, source notes, prototype screenshots and test results show the path between intention and outcome. Capture them as decisions happen rather than reconstructing the process near the deadline.


You do not need a diary of every hour. Select evidence showing what changed, why it changed and what you learned. For Maya, a screenshot before and after user testing, alongside her explanation, makes a design decision visible.


Keep unsuccessful attempts when they explain an important change. An abandoned layout or failed test can support an honest account of learning. Describe what the evidence actually shows, and avoid claiming that a small test proves more than it can.


Review both the product and report. Check quotations, citations, references, image credits, appendices and acknowledgements of tools or assistance. Confirm that readers can connect borrowed material to its source. Use your school’s referencing handbook rather than assuming an online template meets its requirements.


For planning support, explore these[MYP Personal Project resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-myp-resources-personal-project) . RevisionDojo brings together Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, grading tools, the Coursework Library and Tutors to support learning while you retain ownership.


### Keep the project personal


By the end, Maya’s evidence tells a truthful story: what she could do, where she needed help and how her thinking changed. These habits also support the[transition from MYP to DP](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-skills-carry-over-from-myp-to-dp) .


Use RevisionDojo as your IB resource for explanations, planning and constructive feedback. Keep the judgments and final decisions yours, so you can explain both the finished product and the learning behind it.
